l: snow, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Snow is light snowfall, fresh, new-fallen, and white. It falls lightly and softly around Toto's cottage, layering the roof, pump, and windows, then covers the ground, heaps into drifts and shapes, and weighs down forest trees in feathery masses.

l: winter evening, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A winter evening is cold outside but warm and merry inside the cottage, bringing the group together around the fire for supper, conversation, and a story.

l: the supper, Toto's Merry Winter
s: contains the mutton-pie [exceptionally large and richly filled] The supper includes chicken, ham, a large mutton-pie filled with mutton, eggballs, onions, and rich gravy, along with white and brown bread, jam, gingerbread, apples, nuts, cream, and buttermilk. The guests eat with great enjoyment, while the grandmother listens happily to the sounds of their knives and forks.

l: dancing-school, Toto's Merry Winter
s: teaches dancing [to the family] The dancing-school is held in the kitchen after the story of the Useful Coal, with Toto as instructor and the raccoon, Cracker, and Bruin as dancers. The lesson includes bowing, jumping and changing feet, moving forward and back, balancing, turning partners, and waltzing, but ends in confusion when Bruin destroys the custard pie.

l: the grandmother's story, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a story [passed down through two grandmothers] The grandmother's story is introduced as one told to her by her own grandmother. She says that a story passed down through two grandmothers is supposed to be true and begins telling it to the eager group.

l: Chop-Chin, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Chop-Chin is a good twelve-year-old boy, Ly-Chee’s son and an apprentice to the Chief Cabinet-maker, who hopes to become a sweeper. When he learns his father must die, he undertakes a sacred mission: he drugs guards and priests, steals the Golden Dragon, enters the royal palace with the Celestial Footstool, hides in the Dragon to command Emperor Wah-Song, and escapes carrying the Footstool.

l: Ly-Chee, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Ly-Chee, father of Chop-Chin, is a slightly deaf sweeper who has faithfully kept the Imperial court-yard clean for thirty years to protect the Emperor's passage. He accidentally drenches Emperor Wah-Song with ice-cold water, is condemned and imprisoned, then receives the Golden Dragon's pardon. He gains ducats, jewels, and lifelong appointment as Chief Sweeper, and his family rejoices.

l: Emperor Wah-Song, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Emperor Wah-Song, the great and mighty Emperor of China, has a celestial train held up by seven boys and is capricious in going out unannounced. He enters the Imperial court-yard, has Ly-Chee threatened after his clothes are soaked, then mistreats attendants before dreaming of the Golden Dragon. Terrified, he pardons, rewards, and appoints Ly-Chee Chief Sweeper, and becomes meek after his ordeal.

l: Tong-Ki-Tcheng, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Tong-Ki-Tcheng, a powerful prince of the Empire, suffers fever in his palace; Chop-Chin invokes his name to gain access to the Golden Dragon.

l: the four priests of the First Order of the Saki-Pan, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The four priests of the First Order of the Saki-Pan guard the Golden Dragon, the Jewelled Shrine, and the Temple of the Saki-Pan. They drink wine offered by Chop-Chin and sleep while the idol is removed. Awakening to its disappearance, they fear death, then joyfully return the recovered Dragon to the Temple.

l: the Imperial court-yard, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_paved_with white marble [and kept absolutely clean] The Imperial court-yard is a white marble pavement that Ly-Chee and the other sweepers must keep absolutely clean. It is the place where Ly-Chee accidentally drenches the Emperor.

l: the great temple of the Golden Dragon, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The great temple of the Golden Dragon is a sacred destination where Chop-Chin arrives at sunset. It has successive guarded courts and includes the Temple of the Golden Dragon. The Golden Dragon is kept on an altar by four priests, who rejoice when returning it after it is found outside.

l: the Temple of the Golden Dragon, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The Temple of the Golden Dragon is the House of Gold beyond guarded courts, entered through a golden gate; priests lead Chop-Chin blindfolded to its Jewelled Shrine.

l: the Golden Dragon, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The Golden Dragon is the most sacred idol in China, a Fiery Idol worshipped in the Temple of the Saki-Pan. About ten feet long, it stands fifteen feet above the floor on its altar, made of diamond-tipped gold scales, with ruby eyes and an emerald crown. Its faithful servant Ly-Chee brings melons weekly. Chop-Chin steals it from the altar in a crimson sash, then uses it to terrify Emperor Wah-Song into pardoning and rewarding Ly-Chee. Found outside the temple, it is returned by priests, who say it went abroad for the city's welfare.

l: the drugged wine, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The drugged wine, sent by Tong-Ki-Tcheng and presented by Chop-Chin, contains a powerful temporary narcotic; guards and priests drink it, sleep deeply, and allow removal of the Golden Dragon.

l: the Imperial court-yard accident, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The Imperial court-yard accident occurs when the deaf Ly-Chee throws ice-cold water backward as the Emperor steps outside, drenching his yellow satin clothes and damaging his embroidered shoes.

l: Ly-Chee's sentence of death, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Ly-Chee is sentenced by the Emperor to be beheaded at sunrise after soaking the Emperor's clothing and shoes; only the Golden Dragon leaving its altar to beg can revoke the sentence.

l: Chop-Chin's mission to the Golden Dragon, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Chop-Chin undertakes a sacred mission to save Ly-Chee, claims prayers for Tong-Ki-Tcheng, uses wine to pass guarded courts, uses a bronze bowl to enter the shrine, and seeks the Golden Dragon's intercession.

l: the theft of the Golden Dragon, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The theft of the Golden Dragon is committed by Chop-Chin, who at night climbs its altar, finds the idol surprisingly light, wraps it in his sash, passes sleeping guards and the bronze gate, and escapes into the street.

l: the sentinel, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A sentinel at the royal palace’s outer gate, armed with a pike and broadsword, guards the entrance on a dark night, admits Chop-Chin carrying the Celestial Footstool, then lets him leave after a warning against peeping beneath its covering.

l: the royal palace, Toto's Merry Winter
s: has outer gates [closed at night] The royal palace has closed outer gates guarded by a sentinel, though lights remain in many windows. Chop-Chin enters it secretly with the Celestial Footstool and reaches a closet near the Celestial Bed-chamber.

l: the Celestial Footstool, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The Celestial Footstool, a sacred object kept covered from profane eyes, is broken when Emperor Wah-Song throws it, repaired by the Chief Cabinet-maker, carried into the palace by Chop-Chin, and used in a false claim of further damage.

l: the free pardon for Ly-Chee, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_ordered_by the Golden Dragon [to be sent before day-break] The Golden Dragon commands Emperor Wah-Song to send a free pardon to Ly-Chee before daybreak. The pardon is granted, saving Ly-Chee from execution at sunrise.

l: Ly-Chee's appointment as Chief Sweeper, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_ordered_by the Golden Dragon [for life] The Golden Dragon commands that Ly-Chee become Chief Sweeper for life, with gilded brooms, ivory handles, and scrubbing-shoes as yearly benefits. The appointment is carried out, and Ly-Chee is publicly honored in a procession.

l: the Dragon's venture from the Temple, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a venture [the Golden Dragon's going out from the Temple] The Dragon's venture from the Temple is discovered when the four priests see that it is missing from the altar. It is later found outside the gate sitting on its hind-legs with its mouth open, and the priests interpret its return as a glorious journey undertaken for the city's welfare.

l: the Emperor's dream, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a dreadful dream [in which the Emperor encountered the Golden Dragon] In the Emperor's dream, Wah-Song stands in the Golden Temple before the Jewelled Shrine and hears the Golden Dragon call his name. The Dragon accuses him of condemning Ly-Chee and orders him to pardon and reward the sweeper.

l: the Golden Dragon's command, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The Golden Dragon commands Emperor Wah-Song to pardon and reward Ly-Chee and appoint sweepers; terrified by threats, the Emperor agrees.

l: the cellar, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The cellar, beneath a cottage, contains brown mice and is home to Squeak, Scrabble, and their mother. After a frightening kitchen adventure, the young mice return there, while someone seeks to remove the troublesome, thieving mice without killing them.

l: squash pie, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Squash pie is lovely and especially fine; after a remaining piece is left at dinner, two brown mice find it in the cupboard and eat it completely, leaving the plate white and empty.

l: Squeak, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a mouse [little and brown] Squeak enters the kitchen with Scrabble, helps enlarge the cupboard crack, and eats squash pie and hot ginger. After cooling off in a basin, Squeak climbs Bruin, mistakes him for a hill, and flees when he moves.

l: Scrabble, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a mouse [little and brown] Scrabble enters the kitchen with Squeak and helps eat the squash pie and ginger. Scrabble climbs Bruin, whom the mice mistake for a black hill, and escapes with Squeak after Bruin shakes himself.

l: the mice, Toto's Merry Winter
s: live_in the cellar [normally] The mice are Squeak and Scrabble, two little brown mice who live in a cellar. They sneak into the kitchen, eat pie and ginger, suffer from the ginger's heat, cool themselves in water, and flee back home after mistaking Bruin for a moving hill.

l: the mice's kitchen adventure, Toto's Merry Winter
s: involves squash pie The mice's kitchen adventure begins when Squeak and Scrabble enter through a crack under the cellar-door to explore and find food. They eat squash pie, accidentally eat hot ginger, cool themselves in a basin, and then climb onto Bruin before fleeing in terror.

l: the mice's encounter with Bruin, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_caused_by Bruin [while he sleeps on the hearth-rug] The mice mistake the sleeping Bruin for a vast black hill and climb over him. When Bruin stretches, shakes, yawns, and opens his mouth, the mice imagine that they have seen a fiery cavern and rush back to the cellar.

l: woodmouse, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A small brown woodland mouse, distantly related to brown mice, meets <DW53> and Toto on a winter walk, discusses forest room, and invites them to his son Prick-ear’s wedding.

l: Prick-ear, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Prick-ear, the woodmouse's eldest son and bridegroom, begins resenting the raccoon for eating his checkerberries and chasing him, then greets and presents him as a friend at his cave wedding.

l: brown mice, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Two brown mice live in the cottage cellar, troubling and damaging it; they enter at night, gobble squash pie, flee, and are to be sent to the forest.

l: the woodmouse family wedding, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The woodmouse family wedding takes place in the cave on the second evening after the meeting, with many relatives and invited guests <DW53> and Toto.

l: winter walk, Toto's Merry Winter
s: takes_place_in the forest [through fresh snow] <DW53> and Toto take a winter walk from the yard toward the forest after the sky clears. They travel through fresh snow, recall earlier events, and meet the woodmouse.

l: the forest, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The forest is a wild home and beloved woodland place for Toto, the party of friends, brown mice, and many small creatures. It contains Chucky's aunt's burrow, a hollow tree, and a fairy pool. In fresh snow it shows creatures' tracks and homes and offers the brown mice space for a new home. In spring it calls wild creatures back; Toto, Bruin, and the grandmother return to enjoy its pool, greenery, water, birds, and insects.

l: the cave, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A large, low cave is engaged for the woodmouse family's wedding because it can hold their relatives. Its bramble-cleared entrance is flanked by light-wood torches; inside, glow-worms and torches provide light, while holly and alder branches decorate the floor, walls, and corners for festivity.

l: Pigeon Pretty, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Pigeon Pretty is a sober-minded wood-pigeon and the grandmother’s companion, perching on her shoulder during a dancing lesson. She affectionately reassures Bruin about his size. Later, anticipating Baldhead’s fear of Bruin, she brings reviving dried leaves, restores the fainted hermit, and explains Bruin’s kindness so he can welcome the visitors.

l: King Sligo, Toto's Merry Winter
s: King Sligo is a rich, kind-hearted king ruling his kingdom. After repeated treasure thefts, he follows the Useful Coal's instructions, exposes the High Cellarer, and sets the coal in sapphires on his crown.

l: High Cellarer, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The High Cellarer, an officer of the king, secretly steals King Sligo's treasure while feigning investigation; the Useful Coal thwarts him twice, exposes his blackened hands, and leads to his arrest and beheading.

l: the Useful Coal, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The Useful Coal, a speaking, sentient coal, promises to save King Sligo's treasure three times and identify its thief. Burning black and red, it burns and frightens the High Cellarer, reveals him with soot, then dies and becomes a black diamond in the king's crown.

l: treasure-chamber, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A royal chamber holding gold, jewels, and sapphires, protected by King Sligo’s key; the High Cellarer finds the key, enters, steals treasure, and locks the chamber before facing the king.

l: the theft of the king's treasure, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_committed_by High Cellarer The theft of the king's treasure is carried out by the High Cellarer, who repeatedly uses his position to steal gold and jewels. King Sligo stops the theft through the Useful Coal's plan, identifies the culprit by his blackened hands, and finds stolen sapphires and the treasure-chamber key on him.

l: the story of the Useful Coal, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_told_by raccoon [to the family around the fire] The story of the Useful Coal concerns King Sligo's efforts to discover who is stealing his treasure. The coal protects the king's property three times, reveals the High Cellarer as the thief, and is rewarded by being made into a black diamond in the king's crown.

l: the wedding of the woodmouse's eldest son, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The woodmouse's eldest son's wedding occurs in a decorated cave, gathers woodland creatures and the woodmouse's daughters, includes a marriage ceremony, feast, and dancing, then ends.

l: woodmouse's bride, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a mouse [pretty and wearing a brown-fur travelling-dress] The woodmouse's bride is a pretty little mouse wearing a becoming brown-fur travelling dress. She is frightened by the arrival of the raccoon and Toto but takes part in the ceremony and leaves with her husband for their new home.

l: Mr. Woodmouse, Senior, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_father_of woodmouse's eldest son Mr. Woodmouse, Senior, welcomes Toto, Cracker, and the raccoon despite the alarm they cause among the guests. He explains the raccoon's earlier trouble with his son and is relieved when Toto assures him that the raccoon now feels kindly toward the family.

l: little woodmice, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Little woodmice, numerous wedding guests and good people, fear Toto and the raccoon, then recover, dance and feast, make checkerberries and nuts for Toto, and send Bruin regretful apologies.

l: the wedding party, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The wedding party gathers woodmice, field-mice, kangaroo-mice, moles, squirrels, Titmice, Mrs. Shrew and her daughters, and other small creatures. Toto and the raccoon briefly frighten the guests; afterward, they resume greeting, dancing, eating, and drinking.

l: the marriage ceremony, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A distinguished star-nosed mole officiant performs a marriage ceremony: bride and groom eat wintergreen leaves, nibble a third together, and rub noses when they meet in the middle.

l: the wedding feast, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The wedding feast offers nuts, acorns, berries, wintergreen leaves, sassafras-bark, spruce-gum, golden corn, and root-beer in edible birch-bark goblets; guests drink and eat, while star-nosed moles overeat until their stars turn purple.

l: the dancing, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_accompanied_by Toto's whistle [a jig and later a waltz] Toto's whistle leads the wedding party in jigs and waltzes. Cracker dances with a young red squirrel, while Toto and the raccoon perform a waltz admired by the guests; the celebration ends after one final wild dance.

l: comet, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A comet is a heavenly body with a head and shining tail among the constellations. It travels the sky at great speed, though motion may be unseen, disappears, and sometimes returns only after a thousand years.

l: The Naughty Comet, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a story [about comets and disobedience] The Naughty Comet is the story of Short-Tail Comet No. 73, who becomes curious about why comets travel and disobeys the Comet Master's orders. Its disobedience leads to No. 73 being devoured by the Sun, and the story is presented as a warning to the other comets.

l: Comet Master, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Comet Master is master of the comets, directing their assigned journeys and restrictions. Carrying a very long, sharp-pointed stick, he prods and punishes comets that misbehave. He sends Short-Tail Comet No. 73 on a thirteen-week, three-day journey with prohibitions, then orders No. 1 Express to find a runaway meteor and take it to planet Bungo.

l: Short-Tail Comet No. 73, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A young, short-tailed comet assigned a thirteen-week journey seeks why comets travel, disobeys the Comet Master by speaking to a meteor and approaching the Sun, and is devoured.

l: meteor, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Meteor defies the Comet Master, persuades Short-Tail Comet No. 73 to travel toward the Sun, flees after No. 73 is devoured, and is ordered arrested and taken to Bungo.

l: the sun, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The Sun attracts and devours Short-Tail Comet No. 73, making it travel faster and burn, then is replaced by the moon at night.

l: the moon, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The moon, a shining silver globe in the sky, rises after sunset; a young cow mistakes a voice for Bossy’s, leaps toward it, and disappears.

l: Mr. Baldhead, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Mr. Baldhead is an old hermit from Ireland who lives in Baldhead’s cave with a broken, lame leg. Weak, pale, and nearly starving after more than a week confined without food, he begins to recover when water and food arrive. Though he first faints at Bruin’s presence, he welcomes the bear after learning of his charitable mission. He plays Russian backgammon with Bruin, owns and reads books for amusement, shelters Ger-Falcon for winter, and tells Toto, Bruin, and Pigeon Pretty an Irish fairy story.

l: Jim Crow, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Jim Crow is Baldhead's faithful, lame crow companion. Sick and unable to find food, he regains strength after Bruin gives him roast chicken, then leads Bruin and Toto to Baldhead's cave and laughs with them. Later, as Toto's guest, he politely introduces himself at the cottage and escorts Miss Mary indoors.

l: the forest, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The forest is a place of deep woods, ferns, mosses, and a spider’s web, containing the Green Man’s oak-tree and toadstool. Eileen gathers sticks there, encounters the tiny Green Man, escapes the doctor’s house into it, and carefully travels to the oak tree and toadstool.

l: Baldhead's cave, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A lonely cave dwelling with a rustic porch shelters helpless Baldhead, who lies on a rough pallet beneath dim roof-hole light.

l: Baldhead's broken leg, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a injury Baldhead's broken leg has left him unable to move for more than a week. Bruin and Toto bring bandages and medicines intended to help care for it.

l: aid for Baldhead, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Aid for Baldhead brings nourishing food, medicines, bandages, and water to his cave, where Bruin and Toto deliver care for his broken leg.

l: food, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_intended_for Baldhead [as nourishment during his illness] Food is urgently needed because Baldhead has none in his cave and is close to starving. Bruin brings a basket of provisions, feeds Jim Crow a roast-chicken wing, and provides Baldhead with water, jelly, and other nourishing food.

l: robber, Toto's Merry Winter
s: An ill-looking thief with a hooked nose, straggling red beard, and green eyes, he enters a cottage with a heavy robber's pack, steals food and searches for valuables, threatens Miss Mary, then is attacked by a raccoon and scalded, fleeing screaming down the road.

l: robbery and attack, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A robbery and attack unfolds in a cottage when a robber steals food and tries to take silver teaspoons and a porringer. Miss Mary exposes him; Bruin attacks with teeth and claws, and a kettle pours boiling water on his legs. He escapes, after which Miss Mary and Bruin reconcile and thank each other.

l: the attempted robbery of Toto's chickens, Toto's Merry Winter
s: targets the Black Spanish chickens [attempted by Ger-Falcon] Ger-Falcon admits that he tried to carry off Toto's Black Spanish chickens because he was starving. Toto says that people eat their own chickens but do not steal other people's chickens.

l: the hermit's cave, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The hermit's cave houses the recovering hermit and Bruin, hosts visitors and backgammon, and becomes winter refuge where Ger-Falcon is fed and sheltered.

l: the moon-calf, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a calf [said to live in the moon] The moon-calf is described as a calf believed by the young cow to live in the moon. The young cow thinks Bossy has become a moon-calf after hearing the phrase from the maid and the Oldest Ox.

l: the young cow, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The young cow, mother of and very fond of Bossy, grieves when her calf is taken away, believes he is on the moon, leaps toward it, overshoots it, and vanishes forever.

l: Bossy, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Bossy, the young cow's missing calf, is believed by her to live as a moon-calf; she calls to him while trying to reach the moon.

l: The Three Remarks, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a story The Three Remarks is the story Miss Mary tells about a princess who can reply only with three fixed phrases. The phrases are “What is the price of butter?”, “Has your grandmother sold her mangle yet?”, and “With all my heart!”

l: princess, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The princess is beautiful, wise, graceful, and gentle, with black hair and star-like eyes, but can make only three remarks. Pressured by her father to accept a marriage proposal, she leaves to avoid it. Her fixed replies help her expose or outwit a butterman impostor and robbers, gaining rubies and sapphires. She finally accepts marriage with the young king she loves.

l: butterman impostor, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The butterman impostor, a retired butterman, claims an empty throne, is accepted and rules as king, carries a sceptre, then mistakes the princess’s butter question for recognition, pays her six thousand rubies for silence, and leaves the throne.

l: city, Toto's Merry Winter
s: After the late king dies heirless, the city prepares and accepts the butterman impostor as king, then lets him leave and cheers the departing princess.

l: robbers, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A heavily armed, forest-dwelling band of robbers stops a princess, questions her and her bag, mistakes her mangle remark for a countersign, takes her to its chief, and gives her ten thousand sapphires for secrecy.

l: Red Chief of the Rustywhanger, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The gigantic robber chieftain leads Red Chief's band, hides a bag of sapphires in an oak, mistakes a princess's remark for an approaching enemy army, and offers her sapphires and escape.

l: Eileen's escape, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Eileen’s escape begins when Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy leaves and she puts Mrs. O'Shaughnessy to sleep with a monotonous story. She runs across fields into a deep forest, meets robbers after encountering the Red Chief of the Rustywhanger, then follows a ferny path toward open country and the Green Man.

l: young king, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Young king rules from a marble and jasper palace, rides out with his court to catch nighthawks, falls in love with the princess, and proposes; she gladly accepts.

l: marriage, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_between young king [and princess] Marriage proposals are a recurring problem for the princess because she can answer them only with one of her three remarks. She refuses to accept any suitor until she meets the young king, whose proposal she gladly accepts.

l: bag of rubies, Toto's Merry Winter
s: contains rubies [six thousand rubies] The butterman impostor gives the princess a bag of rubies containing six thousand gems, each as large as a pigeon's egg, in exchange for her silence about his identity.

l: rubies, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The rubies are offered by the butterman impostor as a bribe to prevent his exposure. Later, the princess gives one ruby to the young king to show that she is not a beggar.

l: bag of sapphires, Toto's Merry Winter
s: contains sapphires [ten thousand sapphires] The Red Chief of the Rustywhanger gives the princess a bag of sapphires containing ten thousand gems, each as large as a pullet's egg, so that she will follow the route he indicates and not betray his band.

l: sapphires, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The sapphires are the payment offered by the Red Chief of the Rustywhanger to secure the princess's cooperation. Later, the princess gives one sapphire to the young king along with a ruby.

l: the crow, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The crow, the hermit's companion, learns backgammon but cannot lift the dice-box and upsets pieces; afraid of Ger-Falcon, he hides until Toto reassures him.

l: Ger-Falcon, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Ger-Falcon, a wild, lawless hawk and hunted forest outlaw, is the family's present representative, descended from its grandfather seventy times removed. Starving, he pursues Pigeon Pretty; Bruin captures him. After broth, he recounts royal service and stays with the hermit through snow and frost.

l: the winter, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A season especially difficult for Ger-Falcon: it prevents respectable ordinary living; he goes a week without food until the hermit offers feeding until snow and frost pass.

l: the hawk's pursuit of Pigeon Pretty, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_caused_by Ger-Falcon's hunger [after a week without food] Ger-Falcon chases Pigeon Pretty into the hermit's cave, where she is exhausted and falls fainting at Bruin's feet. Bruin captures the hawk before he can pounce on her.

l: the Ger-Falcon family, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a old and honorable race [despite being wild and lawless] The Ger-Falcon family was once trained to pursue, overtake, and kill for the hunting sports of men. Ger-Falcon says that one ancestor served an emperor, but after fashion changed and hawking declined, the family became hunted outlaws dependent on barn-yards and hen-roosts.

l: the fairy story, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_about the fairy-folk [an Irish story] The hermit agrees to tell an Irish fairy story after Toto asks for a tale about fairies. He says that he lived in Ireland as a boy, which he calls the very home of the fairy-folk.

l: Eileen Macarthy, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Eileen Macarthy is a girl of the Macarthy family who lives in the Macarthy cottage with her parents, Honor and Dennis, and her brother Phelim, whom she cares for. A talkative child who loves talking and knows many fairy stories, she pities a grasshopper and later goes into the forest to gather sticks for her mother. There she frees a tiny Green Man from a spider’s web and receives a wish: whenever she speaks, diamonds and pearls fall from her mouth. After she crosses her home’s threshold, the jewels alarm her family. Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy takes her from her parents and holds her prisoner, forcing her to speak continually in his house. Eileen escapes the O'Shaughnessy house by telling Mrs. O'Shaughnessy a long story until she sleeps. She returns to the Green Man and asks that the charm be removed, then goes home with pearls and diamonds in her apron. Her account is believed; she grows into a good, rich woman and marries the young Count of Kilmoggan.

l: the Green Men, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The Green Men are fairies and woodland people who live in the forest. A tiny Green Man, wearing a light green jacket and scarlet cap, grants Eileen Macarthy a wish after she saves him from a spider’s web and sends her good wishes. Later, the Green Men pursue Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy in sport and revenge around County Kerry three times for thrice three days, then let him collapse in a bog and vanish.

l: Honor Macarthy, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Honor Macarthy, Eileen Macarthy’s physically strong mother, anxiously awaits Eileen, mistakes diamonds and pearls falling from her mouth for bewitchment, silences her, and defends her against accusations of stealing the Countess’s jewels.

l: Dennis Macarthy, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_a father [of Eileen Macarthy] Dennis Macarthy comes to the cottage after Phelim calls him and examines the shining objects. He first believes Eileen has swallowed or stolen the Countess’s jewels, then asks Dr. O’Shaughnessy whether Eileen can be cured at home before reluctantly allowing the doctor to take her.

l: Phelim Macarthy, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Phelim Macarthy is a boy in the Macarthy family, son of Dennis and little brother of Eileen. He and Eileen share a trundle-bed, and he depends on her at night. He sees shining objects and calls them marbles, runs for Dennis, and stops Dr. O’Shaughnessy’s carriage so Eileen can be examined and taken away.

l: Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy is a local physician, married to Mrs. O'Shaughnessy, who lives in the doctor's house and owns a narrow gig and old pony. He examines Eileen Macarthy and the supposed diamonds and pearls, dismissing them as glass and trash, judges her seriously ill, and takes her home to attempt an experiment as a cure. He then holds Eileen captive, intending that she speak jewels until his best room is full. Driven by greed, he imagines becoming King Michael and claiming Ireland's crown for wealth, power, and royal glory. When Eily disappears and the jewels become reptiles, his ambition collapses: he flees and is pursued by the Green Men across County Kerry for three times three days, finally falling exhausted into a bog.

l: Mrs. O'Shaughnessy, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Mrs. O'Shaughnessy, Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy's wife, helps guard Eileen Macarthy on her husband's order and greedily gathers diamonds and pearls. Left alone with Eileen on the third day, she falls asleep during Eileen's tedious story, enabling Eileen's escape. She raises the alarm, blames witches, and is violently reproached by her husband.

l: the Macarthy cottage, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The Macarthy cottage is the family’s small home, containing the kitchen, hall, dining-room, and drawing-room. Eileen crosses its threshold before the charm takes effect, and the diamonds and pearls roll across its floor as her family reacts with alarm.

l: the fairy wish, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The fairy wish Eileen chose is a charm that makes diamonds and pearls appear whenever she speaks. The Green Man warns she may want it removed and gives a holly-and-toadstool ritual. Later, he touches her lips with his cap and declares the charm off.

l: the diamonds and pearls curse, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The diamonds and pearls curse makes a diamond and a pearl fall from Eileen’s mouth whenever she speaks. Her family takes the jewels as stolen or bewitched, and Dr. Michael O’Shaughnessy calls them glass and removes her for treatment. Though the fairy’s gift brings misery through his exploitation, it leads to the lesson that loving words and helpful deeds are greater treasures. If Eileen wishes, the spell reversal ritual can remove it.

s: The Green Man's toadstool is a large forest plant at the foot of the Green Man's oak-tree and serves as his seat. When Eileen seeks to remove a charm, she returns there with a sprig of holly, taps or strikes it three times, and speaks the reversal words, causing the Green Man to appear.

l: the Green Man, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The Green Man is a dwindling supernatural fairy at a toadstool beneath an oak-tree. He gives Eileen Macarthy a wish causing diamonds and pearls to fall from her lips, then removes the charm when she returns and teaches that gentle words are pearls and kind deeds diamonds.

l: diamonds and pearls, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Pearls and diamonds are jewels produced whenever Eileen speaks. They fill her lap, the floor, and by the third day the best room to ankle depth, but vanish before Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy sees them. Eily later carries them home in her apron; the Green Man says kind words and deeds are better jewels.

s: is_denied Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy [the Green Man says he has already received his kingdom] Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy intends to use Eileen's diamonds and pearls to become King of Ireland, and he says he may become rich enough to buy Ireland and England. l: royal glory and kingship, Toto's Merry Winter
s: Dr. Michael O'Shaughnessy dreams of becoming King Michael and imagines Queen Victory welcoming him to her throne. He plans to ask her for the loan of her Sunday crown as a pattern, but his royal meditations end when Mrs. O'Shaughnessy announces Eily's disappearance.

l: the party, Toto's Merry Winter
s: A real party at the cottage gathers friends including Toto, the grandmother, Bruin, the raccoon, the old hermit, Chucky, Jim Crow, Ger-Falcon, and birds. They eat, tell stories, play old-fashioned games, and dance to Toto’s fiddle at their merriest, final gathering.

l: spring, Toto's Merry Winter
s: is_approaching the forest [snow melting and weather mild] Spring is said to be approaching because the snow is melting, the sun is warmer, and the air is mild. The prospect excites the forest animals but makes Toto and Bruin uneasy because it signals that their time together is ending.

l: eggs, Toto's Merry Winter
s: are_used_for the custard [fresh eggs gathered from the hens] Toto gathers fresh eggs from Mrs. Speckle and Dame Clucket for the party’s custard. The hens reluctantly give them to him because they are soft-hearted and Toto has not had eggs for several days.

l: the little cottage, Toto's Merry Winter
s: The little cottage, home to Toto, the blind grandmother, and later Bruin, hosts spring farewells, Bruin’s secret stay, and laughing forest-friend visits.

Nurse used to sing of it when I was a child. She sang of the big tree-trunks, standing close together, with their roots intertwining below the earth and their branches intertwining above it; of their rough coating of bark and queer, gnarled limbs; of the bushy foliage that roofed the entire forest, save where the sunbeams found a path through which to touch the ground in little spots and to cast weird and curious shadows over the mosses, the lichens and the drifts of dried leaves. The Forest of Burzee is mighty and grand and awesome to those who steal beneath its shade. Coming from the sunlit meadows into its mazes it seems at first gloomy, then pleasant, and afterward filled with never-ending delights. For hundreds of years it has flourished in all its magnificence,

s: seems at first gloomy, then pleasant, and afterward filled with never-ending delights. For hundreds of years it has flourished in all its magnificence, the silence of its inclosure unbroken save by the chirp of busy chipmunks, the growl of wild beasts and the songs of birds. Yet Burzee has its inhabitants--for all this. Nature peopled it in the beginning with Fairies, Knooks, Ryls and Nymphs. As long as the Forest stands it will be a home, a refuge and a playground to these sweet immortals, who revel undisturbed in its depths. Civilization has never yet reached Burzee. Will it ever, I wonder? 2. The Child of the Forest Once, so long ago our great-grandfathers could scarcely have heard it mentioned, there lived within the great Forest of Burzee a wood-nymph named Necile. She was closely related to the mighty Queen Zurline, and her home was beneath the shade of a widespreading oak. Once every year, on Budding Day, when the trees put forth their new buds, Necile held the Golden Chalice of

s: ing oak. Once every year, on Budding Day, when the trees put forth their new buds, Necile held the Golden Chalice of Ak to the lips of the Queen, who drank therefrom to the prosperity of the Forest. So you see she was a nymph of some importance, and, moreover, it is said she was highly regarded because of her beauty and grace. When she was created she could not have told; Queen Zurline could not have told; the great Ak himself could not have told. It was long ago when the world was new and nymphs were needed to guard the forests and to minister to the wants of the young trees. Then, on some day not remembered, Necile sprang into being; radiant, lovely, straight and slim as the sapling she was created to guard. Her hair was the color that lines a chestnut-bur; her eyes were blue in the sunlight and purple in the shade; her cheeks bloomed with the faint pink that edges the clouds at sunset; her lips were full red, pouting and sweet. For costume she adopted oak-leaf green; all the wood-nymphs dress in

s: ; her lips were full red, pouting and sweet. For costume she adopted oak-leaf green; all the wood-nymphs dress in that color and know no other so desirable. Her dainty feet were sandal-clad, while her head remained bare of covering other than her silken tresses. Necile's duties were few and simple. She kept hurtful weeds from growing beneath her trees and sapping the earth-food required by her charges. She frightened away the Gadgols, who took evil delight in flying against the tree-trunks and wounding them so that they drooped and died from the poisonous contact. In dry seasons she carried water from the brooks and pools and moistened the roots of her thirsty dependents. That was in the beginning. The weeds had now learned to avoid the forests where wood-nymphs dwelt; the loathsome Gadgols no longer dared come nigh; the trees had become old and sturdy and could bear the drought better than when fresh-sprouted. So Necile's duties were lessened, and time grew laggard, while succeeding years became more tires

s: than when fresh-sprouted. So Necile's duties were lessened, and time grew laggard, while succeeding years became more tiresome and uneventful than the nymph's joyous spirit loved. Truly the forest-dwellers did not lack amusement. Each full moon they danced in the Royal Circle of the Queen. There were also the Feast of Nuts, the Jubilee of Autumn Tintings, the solemn ceremony of Leaf Shedding and the revelry of Budding Day. But these periods of enjoyment were far apart, and left many weary hours between. That a wood-nymph should grow discontented was not thought of by Necile's sisters. It came upon her only after many years of brooding. But when once she had settled in her mind that life was irksome she had no patience with her condition, and longed to do something of real interest and to pass her days in ways hitherto undreamed of by forest nymphs. The Law of the Forest alone restrained her from going forth in search of adventure. While this mood lay heavy upon pretty Necile it chanced that the great Ak visited the Forest

While this mood lay heavy upon pretty Necile it chanced that the great Ak visited the Forest of Burzee and allowed the wood-nymphs as was their wont--to lie at his feet and listen to the words of wisdom that fell from his lips. Ak is the Master Woodsman of the world; he sees everything, and knows more than the sons of men. That night he held the Queen's hand, for he loved the nymphs as a father loves his children; and Necile lay at his feet with many of her sisters and earnestly harkened as he spoke. "We live so happily, my fair ones, in our forest glades," said Ak, stroking his grizzled beard thoughtfully, "that we know nothing of the sorrow and misery that fall to the lot of those poor mortals who inhabit the open spaces of the earth. They are not of our race, it is true, yet compassion well befits beings so fairly favored as ourselves. Often as I pass by the dwelling of some suffering mortal I am tempted to stop and banish the poor thing's misery. Yet suffering, in

s: Often as I pass by the dwelling of some suffering mortal I am tempted to stop and banish the poor thing's misery. Yet suffering, in moderation, is the natural lot of mortals, and it is not our place to interfere with the laws of Nature." "Nevertheless," said the fair Queen, nodding her golden head at the Master Woodsman, "it would not be a vain guess that Ak has often assisted these hapless mortals." Ak smiled. "Sometimes," he replied, "when they are very young--'children,' the mortals call them--I have stopped to rescue them from misery. The men and women I dare not interfere with; they must bear the burdens Nature has imposed upon them. But the helpless infants, the innocent children of men, have a right to be happy until they become full-grown and able to bear the trials of humanity. So I feel I am justified in assisting them. Not long ago--a year, maybe--I found four poor children huddled in a wooden hut, slowly freezing to death. Their parents had gone to a neighboring village for food, and had left a fire

But a storm arose and drifted the snow in their path, so they were long on the road. Meantime the fire went out and the frost crept into the bones of the waiting children." "Poor things!" murmured the Queen softly. "What did you do?" "I called Nelko, bidding him fetch wood from my forests and breathe upon it until the fire blazed again and warmed the little room where the children lay. Then they ceased shivering and fell asleep until their parents came." "I am glad you did thus," said the good Queen, beaming upon the Master; and Necile, who had eagerly listened to every word, echoed in a whisper: "I, too, am glad!" "And this very night," continued Ak, "as I came to the edge of Burzee I heard a feeble cry, which I judged came from a human infant. Not far away, screened by the forest, crouched Shiegra, the lioness, intent upon devouring the infant for her evening meal." "And what did you do, Ak?" asked the Queen, breathlessly. "Not much, being in a hurry to greet my nymphs. But I commanded Shiegra to lie close to the babe, and to give it her milk to quiet its hunger. And I told her to send word throughout the forest, to all beasts and reptiles, that the child should not be harmed." "I am glad you did thus," said the good Queen again, in a tone of relief; but this time Necile did not echo her words, for the nymph, filled with a strange resolve, had suddenly stolen away from the group. Swiftly her lithe form darted through the forest paths until she reached the edge of mighty Burzee, when she paused to gaze curiously about her.

In another instant Necile had caught it to her breast and was hurrying with it through the forest paths. 3. The Adoption The Master Woodsman suddenly rose, with knitted brows. "There is a strange presence in the Forest," he declared. Then the Queen and her nymphs turned and saw standing before them Necile, with the sleeping infant clasped tightly in her arms and a defiant look in her deep blue eyes. And thus for a moment they remained, the nymphs filled with surprise and consternation, but the brow of the Master Woodsman gradually clearing as he gazed intently upon the beautiful immortal who had wilfully broken the Law. Then the great Ak, to the wonder of all, laid his hand softly on Necile

s: the beautiful immortal who had wilfully broken the Law. Then the great Ak, to the wonder of all, laid his hand softly on Necile's flowing locks and kissed her on her fair forehead. "For the first time within my knowledge," said he, gently, "a nymph has defied me and my laws; yet in my heart can I find no word of chiding. What is your desire, Necile?" "Let me keep the child!" she answered, beginning to tremble and falling on her knees in supplication. "Here, in the Forest of Burzee, where the human race has never yet penetrated?" questioned Ak. "Here, in the Forest of Burzee," replied the nymph, boldly. "It is my home, and I am weary for lack of occupation. Let me care for the babe! See how weak and helpless it is. Surely it can not harm Burzee nor the Master Woodsman of the World!" "But the Law, child, the Law!" cried Ak, sternly. "The Law is made by the Master Woodsman," returned Necile; "if he bids me care for the babe he himself has saved from death,

Queen Zurline, who had listened intently to this conversation, clapped her pretty hands gleefully at the nymph's answer. "You are fairly trapped, O Ak!" she exclaimed, laughing. "Now, I pray you, give heed to Necile's petition." The Woodsman, as was his habit when in thought, stroked his grizzled beard slowly. Then he said: "She shall keep the babe, and I will give it my protection. But I warn you all that as this is the first time I have relaxed the Law, so shall it be the last time. Never more, to the end of the World, shall a mortal be adopted by an immortal. Otherwise would we abandon our happy existence for one of trouble and anxiety. Good night, my nymphs!" Then Ak was gone from their midst, and Necile hurried away to her bower to rejoice over her new-found treasure. 4. Claus

The nymphs clustered around her and the child that lay asleep in her lap, with expressions of curiosity and delight. Nor were they wanting in praises for the great Ak's kindness in allowing Necile to keep the babe and to care for it. Even the Queen came to peer into the innocent childish face and to hold a helpless, chubby fist in her own fair hand. "What shall we call him, Necile?" she asked, smiling. "He must have a name, you know." "Let him be called Claus," answered Necile, "for that means 'a little one.'" "Rather let him be called Neclaus,"** returned the Queen, "for that will mean 'Necile's little one.'" The nymphs clapped their hands in delight, and Neclaus became the infant's name, although Necile loved best to call him Claus, and in afterdays many of her sisters followed her example

Necile gathered the softest moss in all the forest for Claus to lie upon, and she made his bed in her own bower. Of food the infant had no lack. The nymphs searched the forest for bell-udders, which grow upon the goa-tree and when opened are found to be filled with sweet milk. And the soft-eyed does willingly gave a share of their milk to support the little stranger, while Shiegra, the lioness, often crept stealthily into Necile's bower and purred softly as she lay beside the babe and fed it. So the little one flourished and grew big and sturdy day by day, while Necile taught him to speak and to walk and to play. His thoughts and words were sweet and gentle, for the nymphs knew no evil and their hearts were pure and loving. He became the pet of the forest, for Ak's decree had forbidden beast or reptile to molest him, and he walked fearlessly wherever his will guided him. Presently the news

Presently the news reached the other immortals that the nymphs of Burzee had adopted a human infant, and that the act had been sanctioned by the great Ak. Therefore many of them came to visit the little stranger, looking upon him with much interest. First the Ryls, who are first cousins to the wood-nymphs, although so differently formed. For the Ryls are required to watch over the flowers and plants, as the nymphs watch over the forest trees. They search the wide world for the food required by the roots of the flowering plants, while the brilliant colors possessed by the full-blown flowers are due to the dyes placed in the soil by the Ryls, which are drawn through the little veins in the roots and the body of the plants, as they reach maturity. The Ryls are a busy people, for their flowers bloom and fade continually, but they are merry and light-hearted and are very popular with the other immortals. Next came the Knooks, whose duty

Next came the Knooks, whose duty it is to watch over the beasts of the world, both gentle and wild. The Knooks have a hard time of it, since many of the beasts are ungovernable and rebel against restraint. But they know how to manage them, after all, and you will find that certain laws of the Knooks are obeyed by even the most ferocious animals. Their anxieties make the Knooks look old and worn and crooked, and their natures are a bit rough from associating with wild creatures continually; yet they are most useful to humanity and to the world in general, as their laws are the only laws the forest beasts recognize except those of the Master Woodsman. Then there were the Fairies, the guardians of mankind, who were much interested in the adoption of Claus because their own laws forbade them to become familiar with their human charges. There are instances on record where the Fairies have shown themselves to human beings, and have even conversed with them; but they are supposed to guard the lives of

But the idea of adopting a child of men had never occurred to them because it was in every way opposed to their laws; so their curiosity was intense to behold the little stranger adopted by Necile and her sister nymphs. Claus looked upon the immortals who thronged around him with fearless eyes and smiling lips. He rode laughingly upon the shoulders of the merry Ryls; he mischievously pulled the gray beards of the low-browed Knooks; he rested his curly head confidently upon the dainty bosom of the Fairy Queen herself. And the Ryls loved the sound of his laughter; the Knooks loved his courage; the Fairies loved his innocence. The boy made friends of them all, and learned to know their laws intimately. No forest flower was trampled beneath his feet, lest the friendly

He never interfered with the beasts of the forest, lest his friends the Knooks should become angry. The Fairies he loved dearly, but, knowing nothing of mankind, he could not understand that he was the only one of his race admitted to friendly intercourse with them. Indeed, Claus came to consider that he alone, of all the forest people, had no like nor fellow. To him the forest was the world. He had no idea that millions of toiling, striving human creatures existed.
